Demand from tech giants such as Microsoft, Amazon and Google, all racing to find sufficient clean power to feed data centres underpinning the AI boom, is turbocharging the nuclear revival. Brad Smith, president of Microsoft, explains that even before AI, his firm’s promise to remove more greenhouse gases than it contributed was ambitious. (...) Now, thanks to AI, he reckons Microsoft will consume five to six times as much electricity by 2030 as it anticipated (...). Nuclear power is well suited to data centres because it provides a reliable source of clean energy around the clock, unlike wind and solar. The vast scale of nuclear-power plants also makes them attractive: running an AI data centre can require as much as a gigawatt, which would be provided by millions of solar panels—or just a single nuclear-power plant.

Unfortunately, there are few decommissioned nuclear reactors in America, Europe and Japan suitable for big tech to resurrect. New plants will therefore need to be built. These projects absorb enormous amounts of capital and are sensitive to interest-rate fluctuations and delays. (...) A case in point is the recently opened Vogtle nuclear plant in Georgia, America’s first in decades: it came in far over budget and behind schedule. One way for tech giants to mitigate the risk is to bring in outside investors. Last month Microsoft teamed up with BlackRock and others to launch a $30bn infrastructure fund devoted to AI. Smith expects it to finance nuclear projects, among other things. (...)

At the same time, tech titans have taken a growing interest in SMRs. Currently there are only two in operation, in China and Russia. But Western manufacturers such as GE Vernova and Rolls Royce have been busily developing them, as have numerous startups. TerraPower, backed by Bill Gates, is building its first plant in Wyoming. Oklo, which counts Sam Altman of OpenAI among its backers, intends to deploy several small nuclear plants by 2030. Earlier this year it signed an agreement to provide Equinix with 500 megawatts of nuclear power that includes a prepayment to help fund construction. There are more SMRs planned or under construction in America than anywhere else, thanks in part to enthusiasm from tech. Oracle recently unveiled plans for a gigawatt-scale data centre powered by three SMRs. (...) Sundar Pichai, the boss of Google, confirmed that his firm is also looking into SMRs to power its data centres.

Still, the technology behind SMRs remains unproven at scale. Meanwhile, the uncertain price tag of building conventional nuclear-power plants will continue to weigh on the industry’s growth—and big tech’s hopes of powering the AI revolution without spewing carbon. Chris Womack, chief executive of the Southern Company, reckons that public support would help. “The government must provide some cost-overrun insurance.” Streamlining lengthy permitting processes would be even better. Governments certainly seem to be warming towards nuclear power. (...) Pointing to the surge in demand from AI, the head of the Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation declared: “We have witnessed a step change in momentum.” For it to continue, a mix of technical ingenuity, financial wizardry and supportive policy will be needed.
passages.V2:
Everywhere you turn, there is talk of lived experience. But there is little consensus about what the phrase ‘lived experience’ means, where it came from, and whether it has any value. (...) The Lived Experience Leaders Movement explains that those who have lived experiences have ‘Direct, first-hand experience, past or present, of a social issue(s) and/or injustice(s)’.… In the 1940s and ’50s, existentialists adopted the language of lived experience, coinciding with a turn to identity politics. Jean-Paul Sartre wrote about the lived experience of being a Jew, Simone de Beauvoir about being a woman, and Frantz Fanon about being a Black man. They demanded a return to lived experience, highlighting how dominant cultural categories distort one’s sense of self.

No contemporary philosopher has done more to help us understand identity politics than Charles Taylor. He sees it as a response to the human need for recognition - for one’s most authentic self to be valued. In premodernity, recognition was assured by fulfilling one’s social role, but now it is no longer guaranteed. Hence one’s identity must be acknowledged. Taylor argues that this demand is tied to the romantic notion of a true self obscured by society. Lived experience plays a central role in this process. First, it has become a marker of authenticity. A commonplace is that historical categories don’t match the lived experience of marginalised people. Miranda Fricker calls this ‘hermeneutical injustice’: marginalised people can’t fully understand their social reality because interpretive resources are dominated by the privileged. Talk of lived experience signals authenticity by capturing experiences unreflected in mainstream culture. Second, invoking lived experience has become a way of securing epistemic and political authority. ‘You don’t know what it’s like’ implies privileged knowledge, so others must defer. ‘Speaking as a…’ signals that authority, offering truths that Raymond Williams calls ‘the most authentic kind of truths’. Third, lived experience polices boundaries. Gayatri Spivak calls this ‘strategic essentialism’, in which groups act as if they are monolithic. Kwame Anthony Appiah warns this can create rigid definitions of what counts as ‘authentically’ Black, risking a social prison. … Transgressing these boundaries casts doubt on one’s authenticity.

Those who routinely deploy lived experience politically haven’t been very critical about it. Yet Joan Scott argued that reliance on lived experience can reinforce categories such as ‘Black’ or ‘woman’. Rather than liberating marginalised people, it can entrench the very categories that oppress them. Appeals to lived experience as purely subjective and unanswerable are also questionable. As Kwame Anthony Appiah notes, we can misunderstand our own experiences, distorted by ideology and oppression. Lived experience is never unmediated. Thus, it doesn’t deserve reflexive deference simply because it’s tied to identity or dignity. Refusal to defer may feel like erasure, but lived experience isn’t an unassailable foundation for authenticity.(...)

As bell hooks wrote, identity politics emerges from the struggles of oppressed groups to critique dominant structures. But if lived experience is interpretive, it’s a shaky basis for authenticity. New language may create rather than merely reflect experience. Concepts like ‘Black/white’ or ‘privileged/underprivileged’ shape our self-understanding. If culture shapes lived experience, we must be wary of treating it as our final touchstone.
passages.V3:
Everyone loves to watch hummingbirds—tiny, bright blurs that hover at flowers and fiercely defend feeders. (...) With their small size and blazing metabolism, they live on a knife-edge, sometimes shutting down their bodies to survive the night or migrate thousands of miles. (...) Their nectar-rich diet leads to blood-sugar levels that would hospitalize a human, and their zooming flight can generate fighter-pilot-level G-forces. For years, researchers assumed hummingbirds spent about 30 percent of their day feeding, resting most of the time. But physiological ecologist Anusha Shankar looked closely and found they often work far harder.

Shankar studied broad-billed hummingbirds in southern Arizona, measuring metabolic rates during various activities and estimating total daily energy use. (...) She calculated the per-minute cost of perching, flying and hovering, then inferred how much time the birds spent feeding versus perching. Results varied. Early in summer, when flowers are abundant, they could meet energy needs with only a few hours of feeding, perching up to 70 percent of the day. But when flowers grew scarcer, they perched just 20 percent of their waking hours, devoting the rest—up to 13 hours—to feeding. Hummingbirds have a trick to save energy. When they risk running out, they may go torpid at night, dropping body temperature near the surrounding air. (...) Torpid birds appear almost comatose, breathing intermittently, saving up to 95 percent of hourly metabolic costs during cold nights. This can be essential after days of less feeding or before migration. They still keep their internal clock. (...) To be ready for daylight, they begin rousing about an hour before sunrise, well before visible light cues.

To fuel their sky-high metabolism, hummingbirds may drink up to 80 percent of their body weight in nectar daily—like a 150-pound person downing dozens of sodas. (...) Nectar is often sweeter than typical soft drinks. Humans can’t absorb sugar that fast. Hummingbirds manage it with leaky guts, allowing sugars to enter the bloodstream between cells. This rapid uptake helps them reach blood-sugar levels six times higher than in humans. (...) Such levels would cause severe glycation damage in people, but hummingbirds avoid it—possibly thanks to proteins with fewer vulnerable amino acids. By the end of the night, a hummingbird’s sugar stores are nearly gone. Yet it must wake up and fly. (...) They can rapidly shift from burning sugar to burning fat in mere minutes—far faster than other organisms.

Because nectar is mostly water, hummingbirds must excrete large amounts without losing electrolytes. Their kidneys recapture salts and produce almost distilled water. (...) But if they kept producing such dilute urine overnight, they would die of dehydration. So they shut down their kidneys every night—akin to acute renal failure in humans. Otherwise, as one researcher put it, they’d “piss themselves to death.”
passages.V4:
Confidence is contagious. Someone declaring a position with ringing certainty is more likely to inspire than someone who hedges their bets. “We may fight them on the beaches; it depends a bit on the weather,” would have been a lot less persuasive. A study by Matthias Brauer of the University of Mannheim analysed language used in letters from activist investors; it found that more confident letters were associated with more successful activist campaigns. Confidence confers status. In a study by Cameron Anderson of the University of California, Berkeley, MBA students were asked to take a survey that listed both genuine names and made-up ones. Overconfident students who picked more fictitious entries turned out to have the most influence on their classmates, according to end-of-term ratings.

Confidence without competence will only get you so far. If you go around telling people how much you love “The One Musketeer”, you will not be that influential. But competence without confidence imposes limits, too. Self-doubters are less likely to put themselves forward for big promotions. Irrational levels of self-belief are a hallmark of many successful founders. A recent paper by Terhi Maczulskij and Jutta Viinikainen found that higher self-confidence predicted both entrepreneurship and entrepreneurial success. As much as confidence brings rewards, it also brings danger. Work by Ulrike Malmendier and Geoffrey Tate found that overconfident bosses are more likely to undertake acquisitions. They are also more likely to destroy value. Another paper, by Guoli Chen of INSEAD, looked at how CEOs’ confidence affects their earnings forecasts. Bosses with inflated self-belief were slower to adjust their forecasts when they proved inaccurate. “Put simply,” the researchers conclude, “overconfident executives who make mistakes continue to be wrong for longer.”

In an ideal world, confidence would be distributed evenly and in just the right quantities: an optimally confident person trusts their own judgment while accepting it can be fallible. In practice, confidence is distributed unevenly and is prone to feedback loops. A confident person is apt to place even more faith in their abilities if they have success. One study by Nathanael Fast tested people’s willingness to bet on their performance in a difficult general-knowledge quiz. Those who were asked how much power they had at work before making their bets staked more (and lost more) than others who answered afterward. This messy picture resolves into two propositions for managers. First, puffed-up people need guardrails. A new paper by Priscilla Kraft of WHU finds that overconfident bosses of American high-tech firms have a better record of making breakthrough innovations if they are constrained by powerful, expert boards. Second, self-doubters need encouragement to fulfill their potential. That might come from managers, mentors or even themselves. A study by Joris Lammers of the University of Cologne primed participants in a mock interview to think of times when they had wielded power. Independent evaluators who were unaware of the experiment found that these participants wrote more persuasive cover letters and did better in face-to-face interviews than other applicants. Confidence can be natural. It can also be a trick.

1.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

As the Cold War came to an end, humans were no longer contained within their old geographies or identities. They now inhabited a new world that appeared to be unhinged from the normal evolution of human society. The concept chosen to capture this transformational moment in human history was ‘globalisation’. During the past three decades, more people have begun viewing our ‘global’ world as a cursed fate. With its suffocating time-space compression, globalisation seems to have uncoupled us from the logic and flow of history. Our suspicious, bastard identities - patched together from a mishmash of cultures - appear incompatible with our ancestors’ ‘authentic’ traditions and ways of life. We have become strangers to the places they called home, to the ways they dressed, ate or communicated with one another.
opts: Globalisation, emerging after the Cold War, has compressed time and space, creating fractured identities and estrangement from ancestral ways of life.
As globalisation transformed human existence after the Cold War, people found themselves unhinged from normal evolution, struggling with hybrid identities and cultural dislocation.
The post-Cold War era ushered in globalisation, which severed people from their historical and cultural roots, leading to a loss of authentic identity.
The end of the Cold War brought globalisation, a force that disrupted historical continuity, leaving people disconnected from their past identities and traditions.

10.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

From a humanist position, how do we approach the tech vexed, perfection striving humanity that is fast encroaching right now? What is the antidote to ‘roboticism’, or the transformation of humans into machines? While there is clearly no antidote as such to this problem, there is a sensibility - also growing in stature - that powerfully counters the roboticist trend, and this sensibility is ‘awe’. Awe is the humility and wonder, or sense of adventure, toward living. It has also been defined as a sense of vastness that defies accommodation. However one defines it, the sensibility of awe subverts mechanised living. It demands we live in the present, spontaneously, and with radical openness.
opts: The antidote to the growing roboticism of modern life is the sensibility of awe, which fosters humility, wonder, and a rejection of mechanised existence.
As technology pushes humanity toward roboticism, awe emerges as a counteracting force, emphasizing spontaneity, radical openness, and a deeper engagement with life.
In an age of mechanised, perfection seeking humanity, the sensibility of awe offers a counterforce, encouraging spontaneity, openness, and a rejection of roboticism.
Awe, defined by humility and wonder, serves as a powerful response to the mechanisation of human life, promoting presence and an adventurous approach to living.

24.q:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The anthropologist Clifford Geertz coined the term epochalism to name the anxious discourses of postcolonial states that had attained legal freedom but remained captive to the economic and political power of their former rulers. Much like the old imperialism, the neoliberal past will not be so easily transcended if the structures that it built over decades remain. Careful longitudinal research often reaches conclusions that are as truthful as they are tedious to publics demanding radical change. Even when we are trying to break free, we are always in the middle of history.
